title: Given an array of non-negative values, pick a subset with the maximum total such that no two picked elements are adjacent. Explain the dynamic programming recurrence, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: House Robber (Maximum Sum of Non-Adjacent Elements)

s1_definition.profdef: House Robber selects a maximum-value subset of an array with the constraint that no two chosen elements are adjacent. At each index the best total is the larger of skipping the element, keeping the previous best, or taking the element plus the best from two indices earlier. It is a linear dynamic programming scan solvable with two rolling variables in constant space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India runs promotional cash-back on a row of consecutive days but a rule forbids claiming cash-back on two back-to-back days. We pick the days that maximise total cash-back without ever choosing two in a row.
s1_definition.oneliner: At each element choose the better of skipping it or taking it plus the best from two back.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** House Robber selects a maximum-value subset of an array with the constraint that no two chosen elements are adjacent. At each index the best total is the larger of skipping the element, keeping the previous best, or taking the element plus the best from two indices earlier. It is a linear dynamic programming scan solvable with two rolling variables in constant space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India runs promotional cash-back on a row of consecutive days but a rule forbids claiming cash-back on two back-to-back days. We pick the days that maximise total cash-back without ever choosing two in a row.

**One line to remember:** At each element choose the better of skipping it or taking it plus the best from two back.

sections.s2_technical:
For each index we face a binary choice: either we skip the current value, in which case the best total is whatever it was at the previous index, or we take the current value, in which case we must add it to the best total from two indices back because the immediately previous index is now forbidden. We keep the maximum of these two options. Because the decision only looks one and two positions behind, two rolling variables suffice.

The rolling core is `int twoBack = 0, oneBack = 0; for (int v : values) { int take = twoBack + v; int best = Math.max(oneBack, take); twoBack = oneBack; oneBack = best; } return oneBack;`. A concrete check: with values 2, 7, 9, 3, 1, the best is taking 2, 9, and 1 for a total of twelve, which the scan produces. Senior nuance: the complexity is linear time and constant space; a circular variant where the first and last elements are also adjacent is solved by running the linear scan twice, once excluding the first element and once excluding the last.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India offers daily cash-back on a sequence of consecutive days, but a fraud-prevention rule forbids claiming cash-back on two adjacent days. The analytics team wants to know the maximum total cash-back a customer could legitimately claim across the promotion. Trying every combination is exponential. This is exactly how House Robber works: it finds the maximum non-adjacent sum in a single linear pass.

The code defines a `CashbackOptimizerService` with `maxNonAdjacentCashback(amounts)` using the rolling recurrence. A `Demo` provides daily cash-back values and logs the best total.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is daily cash-back values two, seven, nine, three, one. Step 1: both rolling variables start at zero, meaning no days processed. Step 2: on day two we compare taking two (zero plus two) against skipping (zero), so one-back becomes two and two-back becomes zero. Step 3: on day seven we compare taking seven (zero plus seven) against skipping (two), so one-back becomes seven and two-back becomes two. Step 4: on day nine we compare taking eleven (two plus nine) against skipping (seven), so one-back becomes eleven and two-back becomes seven. Step 5: on day three we compare taking ten (seven plus three) against skipping (eleven), so one-back stays eleven and two-back becomes eleven. Step 6: on day one we compare taking twelve (eleven plus one) against skipping (eleven), so one-back becomes twelve. We return twelve, the best non-adjacent total.

```
  Input: amounts = [2, 7, 9, 3, 1]
    │
    ▼
  twoBack=0, oneBack=0
    │
    ▼ v=2  take=0+2=2  best=max(0,2)=2   → twoBack=0, oneBack=2
    ▼ v=7  take=0+7=7  best=max(2,7)=7   → twoBack=2, oneBack=7
    ▼ v=9  take=2+9=11 best=max(7,11)=11 → twoBack=7, oneBack=11
    ▼ v=3  take=7+3=10 best=max(11,10)=11→ twoBack=11,oneBack=11
    ▼ v=1  take=11+1=12 best=max(11,12)=12→ twoBack=11,oneBack=12
    │
    ▼
  Output: oneBack = 12  (took days with 2, 9, 1)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
House Robber is the canonical maximum non-adjacent sum problem, and the insight is to frame each element as a binary decision. At every position I can either skip the current value, in which case my best running total is unchanged from the previous position, or I can take the current value, in which case I must add it to the best total from two positions back, because taking the immediately previous element is forbidden by the adjacency rule. The answer at each position is simply the larger of those two options.

Since every decision looks only one and two positions behind, I do not keep a full table. I carry two rolling variables, the best total ending one position back and the best ending two positions back, update them as I scan left to right, and the final value of the one-back variable is the answer. This runs in linear time and constant space, which I always contrast with the exponential cost of trying every subset.

At the National Bank of India I used this for a cash-back promotion where a fraud rule forbade claiming cash-back on two consecutive days, and the analytics team wanted the maximum total a customer could legitimately claim. I ran the linear scan over the daily values, and for a wrap-around promotion where the first and last days also counted as adjacent I ran the scan twice, once excluding the first day and once excluding the last, taking the better result. Explaining the skip-versus-take decision, the two-back dependency, and the circular variant is what shows an interviewer I understand this family of linear dynamic programming problems.
